e-6647.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Sums of Exponentials
e-6647.problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t) = e^{-3t}-e^{5t}$ for $s>5.$
e-6647.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
\mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-3t}-{e}^{5t}} & =L{{e}^{-3t}}+L{-{e}^{5t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-3t}}-L{{e}^{5t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
\mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3 \\ L{{e}^{5t}} & =\frac{1}{s-5},\,s>5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-3t}}-L{{e}^{5t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3}-\frac{1}{s-5} \\  & =\frac{(s-5)-(s+3)}{(s+3)(s-5)} \\  & =\frac{-8}{(s+3)(s-5)} \\  & =-\frac{8}{(s+3)(s-5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\mathcal L\{e^{-3t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (-3,\infty)$ and $\mathcal L \{e^{5t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (5,\infty),$ we have that $\mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ is defined for

$$
(-3,\infty) \cap (5,\infty) = (5,\infty),
$$

that is, $s > 5.$

e-21832.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Trigonometric and Hyperbolic Functions
e-21832.problem: Use the Laplace transform of $f(t) = e^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\sinh(3t).$
e-21832.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
\mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\sinh(3t) = \dfrac{e^{3t} - e^{-3t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
\mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3},\,s>3 \\ L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\sinh(3t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{s+3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+3)-(s-3)}{(s-3)(s+3)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-9}) \\  & =\frac{3}{{s}^{2}-9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\mathcal L\{e^{3t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (3,\infty)$ and $\mathcal L \{e^{-3t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (-3,\infty),$ we have that $\mathcal L\{\sinh(3t)\}$ is defined for

$$
(3,\infty) \cap (-3,\infty) = (3,\infty),
$$

that is, $s > 3.$

e-6736.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Combined Functions
e-6736.problem:
Given that for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t) = 3\cos{9t} - 2\sin{9t}$ for $s > 0.$
e-6736.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
\mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{3\operatorname{cos}⁡9t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡9t} & =L{3\operatorname{cos}⁡9t}+L{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡9t} \\  & =3L{\operatorname{cos}⁡9t}-2L{\operatorname{sin}⁡9t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡9t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+81},\,s>0 \\ L{\operatorname{sin}⁡9t} & =\frac{9}{{s}^{2}+81},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =3L{\operatorname{cos}⁡9t}-2L{\operatorname{sin}⁡9t} \\  & =3\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+81}-2\cdot \frac{9}{{s}^{2}+81} \\  & =\frac{3s}{{s}^{2}+81}-\frac{18}{{s}^{2}+81} \\  & =\frac{3s-18}{{s}^{2}+81}.\end{aligned}
$$

L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}} & =L{{e}^{5t}}+L{-{e}^{2t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{5t}}-L{{e}^{2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{5t}} & =\frac{1}{s-5},\,s>5 \\ L{{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{s-2},\,s>2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{5t}}-L{{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-5}-\frac{1}{s-2} \\  & =\frac{(s-2)-(s-5)}{(s-5)(s-2)} \\  & =\frac{s-2-s+5}{(s-5)(s-2)} \\  & =\frac{3}{(s-5)(s-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{5t}}$ is defined for $s\in (5,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (2,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(5,\infty )\cap (2,\infty )=(5,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>5.$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}$ for $s>4.$
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+L{-{e}^{4t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-2t}} & =\frac{1}{s+2},\,s>-2 \\ L{{e}^{4t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4},\,s>4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s-4} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)-(s+2)}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =\frac{-6}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =-\frac{6}{(s+2)(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{-2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-2,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (4,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(-2,\infty )\cap (4,\infty )=(4,\infty ),
$$

content.problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}$ for $s>4.$
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+L{-{e}^{4t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-2t}} & =\frac{1}{s+2},\,s>-2 \\ L{{e}^{4t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4},\,s>4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s-4} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)-(s+2)}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =\frac{-6}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =-\frac{6}{(s+2)(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{-2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-2,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (4,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(-2,\infty )\cap (4,\infty )=(4,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>4.$

\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-3t}}-L{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3}-\frac{1}{s-1} \\  & =\frac{(s-1)-(s+3)}{(s+3)(s-1)} \\  & =\frac{-4}{(s+3)(s-1)} \\  & =-\frac{4}{(s+3)(s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{-3t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-3,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{t}}$ is defined for $s\in (1,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(-3,\infty )\cap (1,\infty )=(1,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>1.$

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions f(t) and g(t), we have L{αf(t)+βg(t)}=α⋅L{f(t)}+β⋅L{g(t)} where α and β are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have L{e−3t−et}=L{e−3t}+L{−et}=L{e−3t}−L{et}.

Next, we recall the following result: L{ekt}=1s−k,s>k

Therefore, we have the following: L{e−3t}=1s+3,s>−3L{et}=1s−1,s>1

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is L{f(t)}=L{e−3t}−L{et}=1s+3−1s−1=(s−1)−(s+3)(s+3)(s−1)=−4(s+3)(s−1)=−4(s+3)(s−1).

Finally, since L{e−3t} is defined for s∈(−3,∞) and L{et} is defined for s∈(1,∞), we have that L{f(t)} is defined for (−3,∞)∩(1,∞)=(1,∞), that is, s>1.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t).$$\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)=\frac{{e}^{4t}+{e}^{-4t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}+{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4},\,s>4 \\ L{{e}^{-4t}} & =\frac{1}{s+4},\,s>-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{s+4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+4)+(s-4)}{(s-4)(s+4)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-16}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (4,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-4,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)}$ is defined for

$$
(4,\infty )\cap (-4,\infty )=(4,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>4.$

EXPLANATION

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions f(t) and g(t), we have L{αf(t)+βg(t)}=α⋅L{f(t)}+β⋅L{g(t)}, where α and β are constants.

First, recall that, by definition cosh⁡(4t)=e4t+e−4t2.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

L{cosh⁡(4t)}=L{e4t+e−4t2}=L{e4t2+e−4t2}=L{e4t2}+L{e−4t2}=12L{e4t}+12L{e−4t}.

Now, we recall that L{ekt}=1s−k,s>k.

Therefore, we have the following: L{e4t}=1s−4,s>4L{e−4t}=1s+4,s>−4

Therefore, the Laplace transform of cosh⁡(4t) is

L{cosh⁡(4t)}=12L{e4t}+12L{e−4t}=12⋅1s−4+12⋅1s+4=12(1s−4+1s+4)=12((s+4)+(s−4)(s−4)(s+4))=12(2ss2−16)=ss2−16.

Finally, since L{e4t} is defined for s∈(4,∞) and L{e−4t} is defined for s∈(−4,∞), we have that L{cosh⁡(4t)} is defined for (4,∞)∩(−4,∞)=(4,∞), that is, s>4.

content.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t).$$\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)=\frac{{e}^{4t}+{e}^{-4t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}+{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4},\,s>4 \\ L{{e}^{-4t}} & =\frac{1}{s+4},\,s>-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{s+4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+4)+(s-4)}{(s-4)(s+4)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-16}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (4,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-4,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)}$ is defined for

$$
(4,\infty )\cap (-4,\infty )=(4,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>4.$

decision.explanation: Using sin(3t)=(e^{3it}−e^{−3it})/(2i), its transform is [1/(s−3i)−1/(s+3i)]/(2i)=3/(s²+9). The defining integrals converge for s>0.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{\text{i}\omega t}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$$\,L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the sine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}-{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}-{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}-\frac{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s-3\text{i}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{1}{s-3\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{(s+3\text{i})-(s-3\text{i})}{(s-3\text{i})(s+3\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{6\text{i}}{{s}^{2}+9}) \\  & =\frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$

content.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Trigonometric and Hyperbolic Functions
content.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{\text{i}\omega t}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$$\,L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the sine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}-{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}-{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}-\frac{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s-3\text{i}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{1}{s-3\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{(s+3\text{i})-(s-3\text{i})}{(s-3\text{i})(s+3\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{6\text{i}}{{s}^{2}+9}) \\  & =\frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{\text{i}\omega t}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t).$$\,L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the sine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)=\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}-{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}-{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}-\frac{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{12\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-12\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+12\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)} & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s-12\text{i}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s+12\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{1}{s-12\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s+12\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{(s+12\text{i})-(s-12\text{i})}{(s-12\text{i})(s+12\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{24\text{i}}{{s}^{2}+144}) \\  & =\frac{12}{{s}^{2}+144},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$

EXPLANATION

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions f(t) and g(t), we have L{αf(t)+βg(t)}=α⋅L{f(t)}+β⋅L{g(t)}, where α and β are constants.

First, recall that the sine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: sin⁡(12t)=e12it−e−12it2i

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have L{sin⁡(12t)}=L{e12it−e−12it2i}=L{e12it2i−e−12it2i}=L{e12it2i}−L{e−12it2i}=12iL{e12it}−12iL{e−12it}.

Now, we recall that L{eiωt}=1s−iω,s>0. Therefore, we have the following: L{e12it}=1s−12i,s>0L{e−12it}=1s+12i,s>0

Therefore, the Laplace transform of sin⁡(12t) is L{sin⁡(12t)}=12iL{e12it}−12iL{e−12it}=12i⋅1s−12i−12i⋅1s+12i=12i(1s−12i−1s+12i)=12i((s+12i)−(s−12i)(s−12i)(s+12i))=12i(24is2+144)=12s2+144, defined for s>0.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Trigonometric and Hyperbolic Functions
content.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{\text{i}\omega t}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t).$$\,L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the sine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)=\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}-{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}-{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}-\frac{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{12\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-12\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+12\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)} & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s-12\text{i}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s+12\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{1}{s-12\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s+12\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{(s+12\text{i})-(s-12\text{i})}{(s-12\text{i})(s+12\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{24\text{i}}{{s}^{2}+144}) \\  & =\frac{12}{{s}^{2}+144},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$

decision.explanation: Since sinh(8t)=(e^{8t}−e^{−8t})/2, its transform is [1/(s−8)−1/(s+8)]/2=8/(s²−64). Both exponential transforms converge for s>8.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t).$$\,L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)=\frac{{e}^{8t}-{e}^{-8t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{8t}-{e}^{-8t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{8t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-8t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{8t}}{2}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-8t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{8t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-8t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{8t}} & =\frac{1}{s-8},\,s>8 \\ L{{e}^{-8t}} & =\frac{1}{s+8},\,s>-8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{8t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-8t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-8}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+8} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-8}-\frac{1}{s+8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+8)-(s-8)}{(s-8)(s+8)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{16}{{s}^{2}-64}) \\  & =\frac{8}{{s}^{2}-64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{8t}}$ is defined for $s\in (8,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-8t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-8,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)}$ is defined for

$$
(8,\infty )\cap (-8,\infty )=(8,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>8.$

content.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Trigonometric and Hyperbolic Functions
content.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t).$$\,L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)=\frac{{e}^{8t}-{e}^{-8t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{8t}-{e}^{-8t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{8t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-8t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{8t}}{2}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-8t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{8t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-8t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{8t}} & =\frac{1}{s-8},\,s>8 \\ L{{e}^{-8t}} & =\frac{1}{s+8},\,s>-8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{8t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-8t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-8}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+8} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-8}-\frac{1}{s+8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+8)-(s-8)}{(s-8)(s+8)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{16}{{s}^{2}-64}) \\  & =\frac{8}{{s}^{2}-64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{8t}}$ is defined for $s\in (8,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-8t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-8,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)}$ is defined for

$$
(8,\infty )\cap (-8,\infty )=(8,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>8.$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t).$$\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)=\frac{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{2t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{s-2},\,s>2 \\ L{{e}^{-2t}} & =\frac{1}{s+2},\,s>-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{2t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-2t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-2}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-2}+\frac{1}{s+2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+2)+(s-2)}{(s-2)(s+2)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-4}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (2,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-2,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)}$ is defined for

$$
(2,\infty )\cap (-2,\infty )=(2,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>2.$

EXPLANATION

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions f(t) and g(t), we have L{αf(t)+βg(t)}=α⋅L{f(t)}+β⋅L{g(t)}, where α and β are constants.

First, recall that, by definition cosh⁡(2t)=e2t+e−2t2.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have L{cosh⁡(2t)}=L{e2t+e−2t2}=L{e2t2+e−2t2}=L{e2t2}+L{e−2t2}=12L{e2t}+12L{e−2t}.

Now, we recall that L{ekt}=1s−k,s>k.

Therefore, we have the following: L{e2t}=1s−2,s>2L{e−2t}=1s+2,s>−2

Therefore, the Laplace transform of cosh⁡(2t) is L{cosh⁡(2t)}=12L{e2t}+12L{e−2t}=12⋅1s−2+12⋅1s+2=12(1s−2+1s+2)=12((s+2)+(s−2)(s−2)(s+2))=12(2ss2−4)=ss2−4.

Finally, since L{e2t} is defined for s∈(2,∞) and L{e−2t} is defined for s∈(−2,∞), we have that L{cosh⁡(2t)} is defined for (2,∞)∩(−2,∞)=(2,∞), that is, s>2.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Trigonometric and Hyperbolic Functions
content.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t).$$\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)=\frac{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{2t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{s-2},\,s>2 \\ L{{e}^{-2t}} & =\frac{1}{s+2},\,s>-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{2t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-2t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-2}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-2}+\frac{1}{s+2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+2)+(s-2)}{(s-2)(s+2)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-4}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (2,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-2,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)}$ is defined for

$$
(2,\infty )\cap (-2,\infty )=(2,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>2.$

Question 11
?

Given that for s>ω, L{sinh⁡(ωt)}=ωs2−ω2,L{cosh⁡(ωt)}=ss2−ω2, find the Laplace transform of f(t)=4cosh⁡(8t)+3sinh⁡(8t) for s>8.

a
s+24s2−64
b
4s−24s2−64
c
4s+24s2−64
d
4s+3s2−8
e
4s+248(s2−64)
Submit

decision.explanation: By linearity, the transform is 4s/(s²−64)+3·8/(s²−64)=(4s+24)/(s²−64), valid for s>8.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Given that for $s>\omega ,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)$ for $s>8.$
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} & =L{4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)}+L{3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} \\  & =4L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)}+3L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega , \\ L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-64},\,s>8 \\ L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} & =\frac{8}{{s}^{2}-64},\,s>8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =4L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)}+3L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}-64}+3\cdot \frac{8}{{s}^{2}-64} \\  & =\frac{4s}{{s}^{2}-64}+\frac{24}{{s}^{2}-64} \\  & =\frac{4s+24}{{s}^{2}-64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11

Given that for s>ω, L{sinh⁡(ωt)}=ωs2−ω2,L{cosh⁡(ωt)}=ss2−ω2, find the Laplace transform of f(t)=4cosh⁡(8t)+3sinh⁡(8t) for s>8.

a
s+24s2−64
b
4s−24s2−64
c
4s+24s2−64
d
4s+3s2−8
e
4s+248(s2−64)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions f(t) and g(t), we have L{αf(t)+βg(t)}=α⋅L{f(t)}+β⋅L{g(t)}, where α and β are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have L{4cosh⁡(8t)+3sinh⁡(8t)}=L{4cosh⁡(8t)}+L{3sinh⁡(8t)}=4L{cosh⁡(8t)}+3L{sinh⁡(8t)}.

We are given that L{sinh⁡(ωt)}=ωs2−ω2,s>ω,L{cosh⁡(ωt)}=ss2−ω2,s>ω.

Therefore, we have the following: L{cosh⁡(8t)}=ss2−64,s>8L{sinh⁡(8t)}=8s2−64,s>8

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is L{f(t)}=4L{cosh⁡(8t)}+3L{sinh⁡(8t)}=4⋅ss2−64+3⋅8s2−64=4ss2−64+24s2−64=4s+24s2−64.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Combined Functions
content.problem:
Given that for $s>\omega ,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)$ for $s>8.$
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} & =L{4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)}+L{3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} \\  & =4L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)}+3L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega , \\ L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-64},\,s>8 \\ L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} & =\frac{8}{{s}^{2}-64},\,s>8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =4L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)}+3L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}-64}+3\cdot \frac{8}{{s}^{2}-64} \\  & =\frac{4s}{{s}^{2}-64}+\frac{24}{{s}^{2}-64} \\  & =\frac{4s+24}{{s}^{2}-64}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Given that for $s>\omega ,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=6\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)$ for $s>10.$
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{6\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)} & =L{6\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)}+L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)} \\  & =6L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)}+L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega , \\ L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-100},\,s>10 \\ L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)} & =\frac{10}{{s}^{2}-100},\,s>10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =6L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)}+L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}-100}+\frac{10}{{s}^{2}-100} \\  & =\frac{6s}{{s}^{2}-100}+\frac{10}{{s}^{2}-100} \\  & =\frac{6s+10}{{s}^{2}-100}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Combined Functions
content.problem:
Given that for $s>\omega ,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=6\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)$ for $s>10.$
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{6\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)} & =L{6\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)}+L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)} \\  & =6L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)}+L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega , \\ L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(10t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-100},\,s>10 \\ L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(10t)} & =\frac{10}{{s}^{2}-100},\,s>10\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Given that for $s>\omega ,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)+6\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)$ for $s>9.$
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)+6\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)} & =L{2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)}+L{6\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)} \\  & =2L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)}+6L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega , \\ L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-81},\,s>9 \\ L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)} & =\frac{9}{{s}^{2}-81},\,s>9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =2L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)}+6L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}-81}+6\cdot \frac{9}{{s}^{2}-81} \\  & =\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-81}+\frac{54}{{s}^{2}-81} \\  & =\frac{2s+54}{{s}^{2}-81}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions f(t) and g(t), we have L{αf(t)+βg(t)}=α⋅L{f(t)}+β⋅L{g(t)}, where α and β are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have L{2cosh⁡(9t)+6sinh⁡(9t)}=L{2cosh⁡(9t)}+L{6sinh⁡(9t)}=2L{cosh⁡(9t)}+6L{sinh⁡(9t)}.

We are given that L{sinh⁡(ωt)}=ωs2−ω2,s>ω,L{cosh⁡(ωt)}=ss2−ω2,s>ω.

Therefore, we have the following: L{cosh⁡(9t)}=ss2−81,s>9L{sinh⁡(9t)}=9s2−81,s>9

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is L{f(t)}=2L{cosh⁡(9t)}+6L{sinh⁡(9t)}=2⋅ss2−81+6⋅9s2−81=2ss2−81+54s2−81=2s+54s2−81.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Combined Functions
content.problem:
Given that for $s>\omega ,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)+6\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)$ for $s>9.$
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)+6\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)} & =L{2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)}+L{6\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)} \\  & =2L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)}+6L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega , \\ L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-81},\,s>9 \\ L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)} & =\frac{9}{{s}^{2}-81},\,s>9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =2L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)}+6L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}-81}+6\cdot \frac{9}{{s}^{2}-81} \\  & =\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-81}+\frac{54}{{s}^{2}-81} \\  & =\frac{2s+54}{{s}^{2}-81}.\end{aligned}
$$
